t.1.119.1: Then the Kṣattṛ, the king, and Bhīṣma, together with their kinsmen, performed the śrāddha rite for Pāṇḍu, an offering full of svadhā and amṛta.
t.1.119.2: Having fed the Kurus and the foremost of the brahmins by the thousands, and having given to the chief among the twice-born heaps of jewels and the finest villages as well,
t.1.119.3: Then the citizens, taking with them those Pāṇḍavas, bulls among the Bharatas, who had performed the rites of purification, entered the city named after the elephant.
t.1.119.4: All the people of the city and the countryside grieved ceaselessly for that bull of the Bharatas, as if for a kinsman of their own who had died.
t.1.119.5: Then, at the end of the śrāddha, seeing those people grief-stricken, Vyāsa spoke to his mother, who was bewildered and afflicted with pain and sorrow.
t.1.119.6: The times whose happiness has passed have come, and dreadful times stand before us; each coming day will be worse than the last, and the earth has lost her youth.
t.1.119.7: A terrible time will come, filled with much deceit, beset with manifold evils, in which the rites and conduct of dharma will have vanished.
t.1.119.8: Go, embracing renunciation, and dwell disciplined in the ascetic grove, so that you will not see the terrible destruction of this family of your own.
t.1.119.11: When Ambikā had said, "So be it," Satyavatī of good vows took leave of Bhīṣma and went to the forest together with her two daughters-in-law, O Bhārata.
t.1.119.9: Agreeing with the words "So be it," she went in and said to her daughter-in-law: "Ambikā, through the misconduct of your son, it seems, the Bhāratas will perish together with their kin, and the grandsons as well; so we have heard."
t.1.119.10: Therefore, taking along this Kausalyā, who is distressed and tormented by grief for her son, let the two of us go to the forest, bless you, if you think it right.
t.1.119.12: Those queens, O best of the Bharatas, having performed most terrible austerities, then abandoned their bodies, O great king, and went to the destination they desired.
t.1.119.13: Then the Pāṇḍavas received the sacraments prescribed by the Veda, and they grew up enjoying the pleasures of life in their father's house.
t.1.119.14: Playing together with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in their father's house, the Pāṇḍavas became preeminent in all the games of boyhood.
t.1.119.15: In running, in snatching the target, in eating, and in flinging dust, Bhīmasena overpowers all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.119.17: Those hundred and one mighty princes Vṛkodara alone would crush, and without great difficulty.
t.1.119.16: In his glee the Pāṇḍava would seize them as they played at crow-hiding, and, gripping them by their heads, he made them fight one another.
t.1.119.18: Seizing them by the feet and striking them down with force, the mighty one dragged them, screaming, along the ground, their knees, heads and eyes scraped raw.
t.1.119.19: Playing in the water, he would seize ten boys with his two arms and stay submerged beneath the water, releasing them only when they were nearly dead.
t.1.119.20: And when they climbed a tree and were gathering fruits, Bhīma would shake the tree with a kick of his foot.
t.1.119.21: Then from the tree, struck by the force of his blows, the little boys, reeling and dislodged, quickly fell down together with the fruits.
t.1.119.22: Never could those boys, competing with Vṛkodara, get the better of him, neither in wrestling, nor in speed, nor in exercises of skill.
t.1.119.23: Thus Vṛkodara, vying with the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, persisted in doing them exceeding harm, out of boyishness and not from a malicious mind.
t.1.119.24: Then the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having learned of that far-famed strength of Bhīmasena, revealed his wicked disposition.
t.1.119.25: In him, who had strayed from dharma and was contemplating evil deeds, an evil resolve arose out of delusion and greed for sovereignty.
t.1.119.26: This Vṛkodara, son of Kuntī, foremost among the mighty, the middle one of the sons of Pāṇḍu, must be struck down by treachery.
t.1.119.28: Having thus made his resolve, the wicked Duryodhana then was ever on the watch for an opening against the great-souled Bhīma.
t.1.119.27: Then, having forcibly bound in fetters the one born after him and the eldest too, Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall rule the earth.
t.1.119.30: And having come to a certain spot, a place at Pramāṇakoṭi, at the end of their play all of them, clad in clean garments and well adorned, slowly ate that food, rich in everything one could desire.
t.1.119.29: Then, O Bhārata, for the sake of sporting in the water, he had large and colourful pavilions of cloth and blankets put up.
t.1.119.31: At the end of the day, wearied from their sport, the heroes, the foremost of the Kurus, chose to spend the night right there in the pleasure-lodges.
t.1.119.32: But mighty Bhīma, exceeding the others in exertion, was then weary, having carried those princes who had come for water-sport; the powerful one, wishing to rest, climbed onto that spot at Pramāṇakoṭi and fell asleep.
t.1.119.33: Having reached a cool resting place, the Pāṇḍava, weary and stupefied by intoxication, lay motionless, O king, and slept as if he were dead.
t.1.119.34: Then Duryodhana, having bound Bhīma with nooses of creepers, quietly toppled him from the bank into the deep water of terrible current.
t.1.119.35: Then, having awakened, the son of Kuntī, Bhīma, the best of strikers, cut through all his bonds and rose up once more from the water.
t.1.119.36: And again, while he slept, he had him bitten by enraged, sharp-fanged serpents of deadly venom on all the vital points of his body.
t.1.119.37: And the fangs of those fanged serpents, though driven even into his vital points, did not pierce the skin of the broad-chested one, because of his firmness.
t.1.119.39: Again he had poison mixed into Bhīmasena's food: kālakūṭa, fresh and potent, carefully prepared, a poison that made the hair stand on end.
t.1.119.40: The son of the Vaiśyā woman disclosed that, out of a desire for the welfare of the Pārthas; and Vṛkodara, having eaten that too, digested it without being affected.
t.1.119.38: But Bhīma, having awakened, crushed all those snakes, and with a backhanded blow he struck down his beloved charioteer.
t.1.119.41: For that poison, though exceedingly sharp, produced no change in him; Bhīma, of terrible build, then digested that too.
t.1.119.42: Thus Duryodhana, Karṇa, and Śakuni, the son of Subala, sought by many means to kill those Pāṇḍavas.
t.1.119.43: The Pāṇḍavas too, those subduers of foes, were aware of all this, yet, abiding by the counsel of Vidura, they did not bring it out into the open.
